title: Keeping ties
hookLine: a relative gone quiet, and a promise about provision and life

cards: Somewhere in a phone there's a family name with no messages since last year. An aunt. A cousin.

A brother, after something nobody brings up at dinner. Families drift without anyone deciding to let them. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, attaches a promise to exactly those names.
In paraphrase: whoever would like his provision to be widened and his life to be lengthened, let him keep his ties of kinship.

teach.h: SILAH: A JOINING. RAHIM: THE WOMB.
teach.b: The phrase is silat al-rahim. Silah is a connection, a joining. Rahim is the womb, and through it everyone you're related to by birth.
The opening verse of surah al-Nisa asks people, in paraphrase, to be mindful of Allah, and of the wombs, the kinship by which they ask things of one another. Then the name inside the word.
In Bukhari, the Prophet says, in paraphrase: the rahim is a branch from al-Rahman, the Most Merciful. Whoever keeps it joined, Allah keeps joined to him; whoever cuts it, Allah cuts off.

The word for family and the name of mercy share their letters, and the hadith turns that into a bond. Then the hard part, also in Bukhari, in paraphrase: the one who keeps ties isn't the one who simply repays in kind.
It's the one who, when the tie has been cut, joins it again. Not the relative who calls back. The one who calls first, after the silence.
In Sahih Muslim, a man complains: I keep ties with my relatives, and they cut me; I'm good to them, and they're bad to me.
The answer, in paraphrase: if it's as you say, it's as if you're feeding them hot ashes, and a helper from Allah stays with you as long as you keep on. And a caution.
Keeping ties doesn't require pretending harm never happened.
What a tie looks like with a truly harmful relative is a question to bring to a scholar you trust.
But the default the hadith sets is the open line.

how: Muslims treat silat al-rahim, keeping ties with relatives, as a religious duty: visiting, calling, helping and greeting family, and reaching out again after a falling-out.

o: honoring only the relatives who are kind to you back
a duty to marry within your own extended family
keeping family ties, even rejoining them when they're cut

p: what a hadith calls the rahim

s: keeping ties means repaying relatives who are good to you
Bukhari: the tie-keeper isn't the one who repays in kind but the one who rejoins a cut tie.
a hadith links keeping ties to provision and life
whoever would like his provision widened and his life lengthened, let him keep his ties of kinship.
a hadith calls the rahim a branch from al-Rahman
whoever keeps it joined, Allah keeps joined to him.

games.q: a man tells the Prophet: I keep ties with my relatives and they cut me; I'm good to them and they're bad to me. what is he told?
o: then you're released from them; let them go.
keep on: a helper from Allah stays with you while you do.
games.why: Sahih Muslim: it's as if he's feeding them hot ashes, and a helper from Allah stays with him as long as he keeps on.

practice: Let one relative come to mind, someone you've let drift, not the hardest one, and see their face. Remember one good thing about them, a meal, a joke, a ride somewhere years ago, and picture the few small words you might send them.
If you pray, you can make du'a for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Silat al-rahim. Keeping the ties of kinship, the rahim a hadith calls a branch from al-Rahman: joined again, even when someone else cut it. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: womb, kinship. keeping it joined is صِلَة الرَّحِم, silat al-rahim.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the ties. Rejoining counts most when the tie was cut. See you tomorrow.
